title: Brent Tumbles 4% as Saudi Signals Partial Pipeline Restart, While Hormuz Transits Collapse to a Record-Low Three Ships
detail: Brent crude fell to $103.61-$103.98 a barrel on Sep 17 -- a roughly 4% drop from the prior close near $108.34 -- as easing concerns over Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline outage offset the crisis's underlying supply risk. Saudi Arabia indicated it could restore about half of the pipeline's lost capacity within days via bypass routes, with full repairs still projected to take up to six weeks; Yanbu's Red Sea loadings, suspended since Sep 15, remained shut. The pullback came even as independent tanker-tracking data showed transits through the Strait of Hormuz collapsing to just three vessels on Sep 17 -- the lowest count of the crisis -- down from 12 the day before and well below the 10-day average of roughly 17, with an empty dry-bulk carrier and a 'dark' tanker running with a disabled AIS transponder the only vessels to cross. The divergence between falling oil prices and near-total shipping paralysis underscored how much of the remaining Gulf flow is now moving through Saudi Arabia's Red Sea and overland routes rather than the strait itself.

media.caption: Brent crude fell toward $104/bbl on Sep 17 as Saudi Arabia signaled a partial pipeline restart within days

title: Saudi Crude Exports Fall 70% as Kingdom Reroutes Around Shut Yanbu Pipeline via Sohar, Suez and the Cape
detail: Saudi Arabia's total crude loadings have fallen more than 70% -- from roughly 7.5 million barrels a day in January-February to 2.1-2.3 million bpd by mid-September -- as the kingdom scrambles to reroute exports around the East-West pipeline, shut since the Sep 10-11 drone attacks, and the subsequently suspended Yanbu Red Sea terminal. The largest replacement flow now moves via ship-to-ship transfers off Sohar, Oman, and through the Strait of Hormuz itself, which Kpler estimated at over 2 million bpd in September's first two weeks despite the strait's near-total shipping paralysis elsewhere; a smaller volume moves north via the Suez Canal and Egypt's Sumed pipeline to the Mediterranean, while the Cape of Good Hope route -- nearly a month longer and roughly four times the distance -- sees only limited use given the cost. At least three European refiners had late-September Saudi cargoes cancelled or pushed back to November; Poland's Orlen said it had purchased 16 replacement cargoes from Norway, the UK, Algeria, Kazakhstan, Azerbaijan and the Americas to cover the shortfall. The East-West pipeline, also known as Petroline, normally carries about 5.5 million bpd, of which roughly 4.5 million bpd is exported through Yanbu.

media.caption: European refiners scramble for replacement crude as Saudi Arabia reroutes exports around the shut Yanbu pipeline
